paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The equilibrium constant of a reaction is the value its reaction quotient takes once the reaction reaches chemical equilibrium. Equilibrium is the state a changing chemical system approaches after enough time, when its make-up shows no measurable tendency to change further.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is useful
paragraphs.text: Under a fixed set of conditions, the constant does not depend on how much of each reactant and product you started with. That makes it a tool for prediction. Know the starting mix and the constant, and you can work out what the mix will be at equilibrium. The value is not fixed for every setting, though: temperature, the solvent and ionic strength can all change it.

paragraphs.heading: Many names, one idea
paragraphs.text: Equilibrium constants help explain many chemical systems. They matter in the body too, in processes such as hemoglobin carrying oxygen in the blood and the steady control of acid and base levels. Several familiar terms are really kinds of equilibrium constant: stability, formation, binding, association and dissociation constants.

paragraphs.heading: Gases and pressure
paragraphs.text: For a gas, the expression uses the partial pressure of that gas in bar in place of its concentration. A mixture of gases at equilibrium can have its constant written in terms of partial pressure or of fugacity. Written that way, gas-phase expressions look much like the ones for solutions, with partial pressure standing where concentration would be.

paragraphs.heading: Acids and pKa
paragraphs.text: In organic chemistry and biochemistry, acid dissociation is normally described with pKₐ values, built using the base-10 logarithm of the acid dissociation constant. Bases are described instead with pK_b, the base association constant. For any acid or base the two are tied together by pKₐ + pK_b = pK_w. So pKₐ alone is always enough for calculations.

paragraphs.heading: Values that shift with pH
paragraphs.text: Some equilibrium constants are conditional. In biochemistry, constants are often measured at a pH held steady by a buffer solution, and different buffers can give different values. A conditional constant for a metal and a ligand varies with pH and peaks at one particular pH. That peak marks the pH where the ligand holds on to the metal most effectively.

paragraphs.heading: Hidden constants
paragraphs.text: Sometimes one chemical formula covers two different forms of a molecule, called micro-species. The constants for each form, called micro-constants, cannot be pinned down from experimental data. Yet how much each site is occupied can matter a great deal for biological activity, so chemists have developed ways to estimate them. For L-DOPA, the isomerization constant has been estimated at 0.9, so its two micro-species are present in almost equal amounts at every pH.
